## Northwest Texas

Most of DSHS Northwest Texas Public Health Region 1 (PHR 1) is rural and frontier. DSHS Northwest Texas has sole jurisdiction over 36 of the 44 counties within the region. These 36 counties cover 43,000 square miles, with an estimated population of 323,747.

DSHS Northwest Texas is a hub for agriculture. We are home to dairies, ranches, wind energy and more. You will also find the second largest canyon in the U.S., Palo Duro Canyon, and the official Texas Bison Herd in Caprock Canyons State Park.

The mission of DSHS Northwest Texas is to support the health of our communities. We provide public health consultation, education, promotion, prevention, treatment, and regulation.

## Northwest Texas

Most of DSHS Northwest Texas Public Health Region 1 (PHR 1) is rural and frontier. DSHS Northwest Texas has sole jurisdiction over 36 of the 44 counties within the region. These 36 counties cover 43,000 square miles, with an estimated population of 323,747.

DSHS Northwest Texas is a hub for agriculture. We are home to dairies, ranches, wind energy and more. You will also find the second largest canyon in the U.S., Palo Duro Canyon, and the official Texas Bison Herd in Caprock Canyons State Park.

The mission of DSHS Northwest Texas is to support the health of our communities. We provide public health consultation, education, promotion, prevention, treatment, and regulation.

# Regional and Local Health Operations

The Division of Regional and Local Health Operations (RLHO) serves Texans in their communities. RLHO provides public health services, supports local health agencies, and helps with emergencies.

RLHO is responsible for:

*   All local DSHS public health offices
*   [Office of Border Public Health](https://www.dshs.texas.gov/borderhealth/)
*   [Center for Health Emergency Preparedness and Response](https://www.dshs.texas.gov/about-the-center-health-emergency-preparedness-response)
*   [Texas Center for Infectious Disease](https://www.dshs.texas.gov/regional-local-health-operations/texas-center-infectious-disease) -a hospital specializing in tuberculosis and Hansen's Disease

# Regional and Local Health Operations

The Division of Regional and Local Health Operations (RLHO) serves Texans in their communities. RLHO provides public health services, supports local health agencies, and helps with emergencies.

RLHO is responsible for:

*   All local DSHS public health offices
*   [Office of Border Public Health](https://www.dshs.texas.gov/borderhealth/)
*   [Center for Health Emergency Preparedness and Response](https://www.dshs.texas.gov/about-the-center-health-emergency-preparedness-response)
*   [Texas Center for Infectious Disease](https://www.dshs.texas.gov/regional-local-health-operations/texas-center-infectious-disease) -a hospital specializing in tuberculosis and Hansen's Disease

PHRs are the local presence of DSHS and work in communities to serve the public health needs of Texas, help screen Texans for diseases and connect them to needed services, and provide medical response during public health and weather emergencies.

Our first stop takes us to PHR 4/5N in East Texas. This PHR includes 35 counties and 175 DSHS employees who proudly serve y’all. Better known as the Piney Woods, this region is home to three of the state’s five national forests ![Image 2: 🌲](https://static.xx.fbcdn.net/images/emoji.php/v9/tea/1/16/1f332.png)

Tyler is also famous for its agricultural production. That includes meat processing facilities that DSHS inspects. Our inspectors make sure products come from healthy animals that are humanely slaughtered in a sanitary environment.

**Texas Department of State Health Services** is a state agency of [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas"). The department was created by House Bill 2292 of the 78th Texas Legislature in 2003 through the merging of four state agencies: the Texas Department of Health, Texas Department of Mental Health and Mental Retardation, Texas Health Care Information Council, and [Texas Commission on Alcohol and Drug Abuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Commission_on_Alcohol_and_Drug_Abuse "Texas Commission on Alcohol and Drug Abuse").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-1) The department provides state-operated health care services, including hospitals, health centers, and health agencies. The agency is headquartered at the Central Campus at 1100 West 49th Street in [Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-2) The DSHS Council governs the department.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-3)

The agency's Mental Health and Substance Abuse Division, along with Public Policy Research Institute at [Texas A&M University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_A&M_University "Texas A&M University") coordinate the Texas School Survey,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-4) a program consisting of two surveys on drug and alcohol abuse, an annual one done at the local school-district level and a biennial statewide survey. The statewide survey, called the Texas School Survey of Substance Use, is the largest survey of its kind to be conducted in the United States and administered to over 100,000 public school students between grades 7–12.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-6)

## Leadership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Leadership")]

Dr. Jennifer Shuford is the Commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services. She was appointed to this position in December 2022. [[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-7)

## Geographic structure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geographic structure")]

The agency provides an array of public health services and oversight across the state through eight regional offices.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-10)

*   Region 1 - Lubbock
*   Region 2/3 - Arlington
*   Region 4/5 North - Tyler
*   Region 6/5 South - Houston
*   Region 7 - Temple
*   Region 8 - San Antonio
*   Region 9/10 - El Paso
*   Region 11 - Harlingen

**Texas Department of State Health Services** is a state agency of [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas"). The department was created by House Bill 2292 of the 78th Texas Legislature in 2003 through the merging of four state agencies: the Texas Department of Health, Texas Department of Mental Health and Mental Retardation, Texas Health Care Information Council, and [Texas Commission on Alcohol and Drug Abuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Commission_on_Alcohol_and_Drug_Abuse "Texas Commission on Alcohol and Drug Abuse").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-1) The department provides state-operated health care services, including hospitals, health centers, and health agencies. The agency is headquartered at the Central Campus at 1100 West 49th Street in [Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-2) The DSHS Council governs the department.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-3)

The agency's Mental Health and Substance Abuse Division, along with Public Policy Research Institute at [Texas A&M University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_A&M_University "Texas A&M University") coordinate the Texas School Survey,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-4) a program consisting of two surveys on drug and alcohol abuse, an annual one done at the local school-district level and a biennial statewide survey. The statewide survey, called the Texas School Survey of Substance Use, is the largest survey of its kind to be conducted in the United States and administered to over 100,000 public school students between grades 7–12.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-6)

## Leadership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Leadership")]

Dr. Jennifer Shuford is the Commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services. She was appointed to this position in December 2022. [[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-7)

## Geographic structure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geographic structure")]

The agency provides an array of public health services and oversight across the state through eight regional offices.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Department_of_State_Health_Services#cite_note-10)

*   Region 1 - Lubbock
*   Region 2/3 - Arlington
*   Region 4/5 North - Tyler
*   Region 6/5 South - Houston
*   Region 7 - Temple
*   Region 8 - San Antonio
*   Region 9/10 - El Paso
*   Region 11 - Harlingen

## Central Texas

DSHS Central Texas Public Health Region (PHR) 7 includes 30 counties. The area is about 25,830 square miles, or 16.5 million acres. It has both small towns and big cities, stretching from the Texas Hill Country to the prairies. DSHS Central Texas is known for its cultural heritage, natural beauty, and as being home to the state capital.

DSHS Central Texas works with the eight local health departments. Together, we keep track of community health, help people stay healthier, and respond to public health emergencies. The other 22 counties do not have their own health department, which makes DSHS Central Texas an important resource. Our staff works to keep food safe, stop the spread of disease and connect families with resources.

## Central Texas

DSHS Central Texas Public Health Region (PHR) 7 includes 30 counties. The area is about 25,830 square miles, or 16.5 million acres. It has both small towns and big cities, stretching from the Texas Hill Country to the prairies. DSHS Central Texas is known for its cultural heritage, natural beauty, and as being home to the state capital.

DSHS Central Texas works with the eight local health departments. Together, we keep track of community health, help people stay healthier, and respond to public health emergencies. The other 22 counties do not have their own health department, which makes DSHS Central Texas an important resource. Our staff works to keep food safe, stop the spread of disease and connect families with resources.

## Northwest Texas

Most of DSHS Northwest Texas Public Health Region 1 (PHR 1) is rural and frontier. DSHS Northwest Texas has sole jurisdiction over 36 of the 44 counties within the region. These 36 counties cover 43,000 square miles, with an estimated population of 323,747.

DSHS Northwest Texas is a hub for agriculture. We are home to dairies, ranches, wind energy and more. You will also find the second largest canyon in the U.S., Palo Duro Canyon, and the official Texas Bison Herd in Caprock Canyons State Park.

The mission of DSHS Northwest Texas is to support the health of our communities. We provide public health consultation, education, promotion, prevention, treatment, and regulation.

## Northwest Texas

Most of DSHS Northwest Texas Public Health Region 1 (PHR 1) is rural and frontier. DSHS Northwest Texas has sole jurisdiction over 36 of the 44 counties within the region. These 36 counties cover 43,000 square miles, with an estimated population of 323,747.

DSHS Northwest Texas is a hub for agriculture. We are home to dairies, ranches, wind energy and more. You will also find the second largest canyon in the U.S., Palo Duro Canyon, and the official Texas Bison Herd in Caprock Canyons State Park.

The mission of DSHS Northwest Texas is to support the health of our communities. We provide public health consultation, education, promotion, prevention, treatment, and regulation.

# Public Health

## Our Commitment to Lubbock

Our mission is to improve and protect the health of our community by providing holistic services founded on evidence-based practices. We strive to bridge the gap in assistance for the underserved, facilitate community partnerships, and advocate physical and social wellness.

Our vision is to be the catalyst of a citywide collaboration that empowers citizens to prioritize, achieve, and maintain optimal health.

## ![Image 6: front desk employees working](https://www.mylubbock.us/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=7484)What is Public Health?

Public health is the work of protecting and improving the health of people in communities. While hospitals and clinics treat people who are sick, public health works to keep people from getting sick in the first place. It's the work that often happens in the background such as tracking disease outbreaks, making sure restaurants are safe, connecting people to services, and preparing our community to respond when emergencies arise. When public health is working well, most people never notice it.

Think about it this way: when you get a flu shot, drink clean water, or eat at a restaurant with a clean inspection score, public health made that possible. When a disease outbreak is caught early and contained before it spreads, that's public health. When someone who doesn't know where to turn finds their way to care, that's public health too. Public health also complements the health care system by addressing gaps in care when private care is unavailable or financially out of reach.

At Lubbock Public Health, that work looks like immunizations, STI testing and treatment, HIV services, behavioral health support and disease surveillance — among others. We serve people across the full spectrum of need, and our clinical services are a core part of how we do that.

Lubbock Public Health is a city-county department funded through a combination of local tax dollars,state funding, and federal grants that support programs across all of these service areas. Local investment is the foundation that holds everything together — it gives us the flexibility to respond to the unexpected, fill gaps that grant funding doesn't cover, and keep our doors open for everyone in this community regardless of their ability to pay.

Public health infrastructure isn't visible the way a road or a fire station is, but it is just as essential. The team at Lubbock Public Health is here every day — ready to serve, ready to respond, and committed to keeping our community healthy.

## Message from the Director

Welcome to Lubbock Pu![Image 7: KWells HeadShot Feb 2026](https://www.mylubbock.us/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=7518)blic Health. It is my privilege to serve the residents of Lubbock and Lubbock County, and I am proud to lead a team that shows up every day for this community.

Our department provides clinical services, disease surveillance, emergency preparedness, and population health programs for the people who call Lubbock home. When I became director more than a decade ago, our department had ten employees. Today we have more than 55 dedicated professionals working alongside community partners, health systems, and local leaders to make Lubbock a healthier place to live, work, and raise a family.

We believe a strong local health department plays a vital role in serving the entire community by identifying and addressing gaps in care, ensuring that individuals who might otherwise be overlooked are connected to the information, services, and resources necessary to support their health and well‑being. Whether that's a vaccine, a behavioral health referral, a disease intervention, or a conversation with someone who just needs to know where to turn, we want every person who walks through our doors to know that we are here for them.

We are also proud of what this community has built together. Our facility near 50th and Avenue U opened in 2023 and was made possible through the investment of both the City of Lubbock and Lubbock County. It reflects what we believe public health should feel like — welcoming, modern, and built around the people we serve.

Our mission is to promote a healthy Lubbock by providing and supporting essential public health services throughout our community. I am honored to do that work alongside an exceptional team and the partners and residents who make it possible. For more information on our work and priorities read our [community needs assessment (PDF)](https://www.mylubbock.us/DocumentCenter/View/2567).

Katherine Wells, DrPH, MPH

# Directory of Local Health Departments

NACCHO has created a tool to help you search for local health departments in your area. Find contact information for local health departments using the map below and check to see that your health department is listed correctly.

If you are part of a local health department and need to update your information displayed in the map below, log in using your [MyNACCHO](http://eweb.naccho.org/eweb/DynamicPage.aspx?WebCode=LoginRequired&expires=yes&Site=NACCHO) account to make sure we have your team’s correct contact information. For any questions or help with your MyNACCHO account, email [membership@naccho.org](mailto:membership@naccho.org)

## Northwest Texas

Most of DSHS Northwest Texas Public Health Region 1 (PHR 1) is rural and frontier. DSHS Northwest Texas has sole jurisdiction over 36 of the 44 counties within the region. These 36 counties cover 43,000 square miles, with an estimated population of 323,747.

DSHS Northwest Texas is a hub for agriculture. We are home to dairies, ranches, wind energy and more. You will also find the second largest canyon in the U.S., Palo Duro Canyon, and the official Texas Bison Herd in Caprock Canyons State Park.

The mission of DSHS Northwest Texas is to support the health of our communities. We provide public health consultation, education, promotion, prevention, treatment, and regulation.

## Northwest Texas

Most of DSHS Northwest Texas Public Health Region 1 (PHR 1) is rural and frontier. DSHS Northwest Texas has sole jurisdiction over 36 of the 44 counties within the region. These 36 counties cover 43,000 square miles, with an estimated population of 323,747.

DSHS Northwest Texas is a hub for agriculture. We are home to dairies, ranches, wind energy and more. You will also find the second largest canyon in the U.S., Palo Duro Canyon, and the official Texas Bison Herd in Caprock Canyons State Park.

The mission of DSHS Northwest Texas is to support the health of our communities. We provide public health consultation, education, promotion, prevention, treatment, and regulation.

# Regional and Local Health Operations

The Division of Regional and Local Health Operations (RLHO) serves Texans in their communities. RLHO provides public health services, supports local health agencies, and helps with emergencies.

RLHO is responsible for:

*   All local DSHS public health offices
*   [Office of Border Public Health](https://www.dshs.texas.gov/borderhealth/)
*   [Center for Health Emergency Preparedness and Response](https://www.dshs.texas.gov/about-the-center-health-emergency-preparedness-response)
*   [Texas Center for Infectious Disease](https://www.dshs.texas.gov/regional-local-health-operations/texas-center-infectious-disease) -a hospital specializing in tuberculosis and Hansen's Disease

# Regional and Local Health Operations

The Division of Regional and Local Health Operations (RLHO) serves Texans in their communities. RLHO provides public health services, supports local health agencies, and helps with emergencies.

RLHO is responsible for:

*   All local DSHS public health offices
*   [Office of Border Public Health](https://www.dshs.texas.gov/borderhealth/)
*   [Center for Health Emergency Preparedness and Response](https://www.dshs.texas.gov/about-the-center-health-emergency-preparedness-response)
*   [Texas Center for Infectious Disease](https://www.dshs.texas.gov/regional-local-health-operations/texas-center-infectious-disease) -a hospital specializing in tuberculosis and Hansen's Disease

## North Central Texas

Nearly 8 million people live in DSHS North Central Texas Public Health Region (PHR) 2/3, which includes the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex. If DSHS North Central Texas was its own state, we would be the 14th largest state based on population size.

DSHS North Central Texas is home to 49 counties, some are urban, most are rural, and a few are frontier. We are the public health services provider for 37 counties. For the other 12 counties, we work together with their local health departments. To serve a region of this size, DSHS North Central Texas has nine field offices, a headquarters and several smaller offices.

Our mission is to improve the health, safety, and well-being of Texans in North Central Texas.

## North Central Texas

Nearly 8 million people live in DSHS North Central Texas Public Health Region (PHR) 2/3, which includes the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex. If DSHS North Central Texas was its own state, we would be the 14th largest state based on population size.

DSHS North Central Texas is home to 49 counties, some are urban, most are rural, and a few are frontier. We are the public health services provider for 37 counties. For the other 12 counties, we work together with their local health departments. To serve a region of this size, DSHS North Central Texas has nine field offices, a headquarters and several smaller offices.

Our mission is to improve the health, safety, and well-being of Texans in North Central Texas.

## West Texas

DSHS West Texas Public Health Region (PHR) 9/10 covers more than 86,000 square miles across 35 counties, making it the largest public health region in the state. The area includes a mix of art communities, oil and gas fields, ranches and desert landscapes. A large part of the region falls along the Texas-Mexico border. About 5.6 million people cross the border every year to work, shop, and visit loved ones.

This part of Texas has unique challenges because of its size and diverse landscape. To tackle these challenges, DSHS West Texas staff build strong relationships with community partners. Together, we provide access to health services, disaster relief and more.

## West Texas

DSHS West Texas Public Health Region (PHR) 9/10 covers more than 86,000 square miles across 35 counties, making it the largest public health region in the state. The area includes a mix of art communities, oil and gas fields, ranches and desert landscapes. A large part of the region falls along the Texas-Mexico border. About 5.6 million people cross the border every year to work, shop, and visit loved ones.

This part of Texas has unique challenges because of its size and diverse landscape. To tackle these challenges, DSHS West Texas staff build strong relationships with community partners. Together, we provide access to health services, disaster relief and more.

## Piney Woods

The aptly named DSHS Piney Woods Public Health Region (PHR) 4/5N is home to three of the state’s five national forests!

DSHS Piney Woods includes the city of Tyler, which was the first-ever headquarters of a public health region. It was established in 1970 as part of what was then called the Texas Department of Health. Tyler is also famous for its agriculture and is known as the "Rose Capital of the United States." It also is home to meat processing facilities that DSHS inspects. Our inspectors make sure healthy animals are humanely slaughtered in a sanitary environment.

## Piney Woods

The aptly named DSHS Piney Woods Public Health Region (PHR) 4/5N is home to three of the state’s five national forests!

DSHS Piney Woods includes the city of Tyler, which was the first-ever headquarters of a public health region. It was established in 1970 as part of what was then called the Texas Department of Health. Tyler is also famous for its agriculture and is known as the "Rose Capital of the United States." It also is home to meat processing facilities that DSHS inspects. Our inspectors make sure healthy animals are humanely slaughtered in a sanitary environment.

## South Texas

DSHS South Texas Public Health Region (PHR) 11 is a region rich in history and traditions, and is famous for its warm weather, tropical beaches, birding sites and many palm trees. Also known as the Rio Grande Valley (RGV), this area is home to nine bridges connecting the RGV to Mexico. The RGV is also one of the fastest-growing areas in the U.S.

The work of DSHS South Texas includes tracking human and animal disease outbreaks and preventing foodborne illness. We also help people find health services and education. Our region is also subject to extreme weather events including hurricanes and floods. Each response requires effective communication and collaboration with regional and state partners.

DSHS South Texas is also where the first-ever DSHS Oral Rabies Vaccination Program launched in 1995. Every year, flights take off from Edinburg (as well as Del Rio and Van Horn) and drop more than 1 million vaccine baits along the Texas-Mexico border. These vaccines help stop the spread of rabies. Baits are placed in small, plastic packets that resemble fast-food ketchup. Baits are dipped in fish oil and coated with fish-meal crumbles to attract wildlife. Remember, if you come across one of these packets, leave it alone.

## South Texas

DSHS South Texas Public Health Region (PHR) 11 is a region rich in history and traditions, and is famous for its warm weather, tropical beaches, birding sites and many palm trees. Also known as the Rio Grande Valley (RGV), this area is home to nine bridges connecting the RGV to Mexico. The RGV is also one of the fastest-growing areas in the U.S.

The work of DSHS South Texas includes tracking human and animal disease outbreaks and preventing foodborne illness. We also help people find health services and education. Our region is also subject to extreme weather events including hurricanes and floods. Each response requires effective communication and collaboration with regional and state partners.

DSHS South Texas is also where the first-ever DSHS Oral Rabies Vaccination Program launched in 1995. Every year, flights take off from Edinburg (as well as Del Rio and Van Horn) and drop more than 1 million vaccine baits along the Texas-Mexico border. These vaccines help stop the spread of rabies. Baits are placed in small, plastic packets that resemble fast-food ketchup. Baits are dipped in fish oil and coated with fish-meal crumbles to attract wildlife. Remember, if you come across one of these packets, leave it alone.

Abstract: The goal of this research was to survey the state of the regulatory environment and common practices in other state DOTs to learn how other states deal with the issue of lead-based paint and asbestos-containing materials in bridge maintenance and repair for the state’s 32,000 existing bridges. The survey included 40 questions to all 50 state DOTs, with 39 respond ing. The survey responses were eval uated to formulate primary recommendatio ns intended to decrease TxDOT liabil ity in the short term. Among the primary reco mmendations were to t rain TxDOT personnel on appropriate OSHA regulations, limit TxDOT worker exposure to hazardous materials, and establish oversight of contractor controls and safety prot ocols. The study also led to several secondary recommendati ons to designed to limit TxDOT liability in the long term, such as conducting a study of all bridges to determine the exact location, quantity, and nature of both LBP and ACM, conduct a study of ambient air monitors to measure airborne lead concentrations, and determine the economics of encasing ACM and LBP wastes in concrete. 17.
